quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the vocabulary of a stitching order costing sheet: ratings, grades, rags, proceeds, loading and allocated fixed cost.

questions.q: What does the linear rating of an item express?
options: Pieces produced per operator per hour
Metres of fabric consumed per finished piece
Metres of fabric per bag of yarn
questions.explain: The linear rating (from Lecture 25) is the metres of fabric one piece takes; A-grade pieces × rating gives the fabric in good pieces. Output per operator is a different measure altogether.

questions.q: In the order sheet, fabric consumed by an item is the sum of:
options: A-grade fabric, B-grade fabric and rags
questions.explain: All fabric issued is charged to the item: the metres in A-grade pieces, the metres in B-grade pieces and the rags. Charging only the A-grade metres would understate the fabric cost.

questions.q: The yield of an item in this sheet is:
options: Fabric in A-grade pieces ÷ total fabric consumed
questions.explain: Yield is the A-grade share of the fabric consumed (96.3 % in the pillow-case example); the remaining 3.7 % is wastage, made up of B-grade fabric and rags.

questions.q: B-grade proceeds and rag proceeds are added to the cost of the item.
questions.explain: They are credits: the money recovered by selling B-grade pieces and rags is deducted from the fabric cost, reducing the variable cost of the A-grade pieces.

questions.q: Rag proceeds in the lecture are valued at:
options: The full fabric rate per metre
15 % of the fabric rate per metre
questions.explain: Rags are sold at 15 % of the fabric rate: 25 m × 15 % × Rs 167 = Rs 626.25. Rs 15 per piece is the B-grade proceed, a different credit.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT part of the total variable manufacturing cost in the sheet?
questions.explain: Fixed cost is added after the variable total, as an allocation of 3.2 × direct labour; accessories, labour and loading are all variable with the order.

questions.q: How is fixed cost allocated to an item in this lecture?
options: Equally per piece across the whole order
As a percentage of the fabric cost
As a multiple (3.2 ×) of the item's direct labour
questions.explain: Fixed cost allocated = 3.2 × direct labour; for the pillow case Rs 2,131.20 × 3.2 = Rs 6,819.84. The multiplier is an input cell so the rate can be changed.

questions.q: In the eight-item order the two large comforter-shell lines are the only reason the order as a whole shows a profit.
questions.explain: Items 3 and 4 earn about Rs 100,000 and Rs 170,000; every pillow item and the two small comforter lines of 210 pieces lose or earn little, so the grand total of Rs 240,693 rests on those two lines.

questions.q: The costing sheet shows per-piece figures in one column and order totals in another. The per-piece fabric cost is calculated over:
questions.explain: Only A-grade pieces are sold at the full price, so the whole fabric cost (net of proceeds) is spread over the 1,776 A-grade pieces: Rs 132,427.66 ÷ 1,776 = Rs 74.57.

questions.q: Why does the lecture mention Activity Based Costing at the end of the order sheet?
options: To calculate the linear rating more accurately
To test whether allocating fixed cost at 3.2 × labour gives small labour-heavy pieces a fair share of overhead
To reduce the fabric rate per metre
To replace the sales price with a cost-plus price
questions.explain: Labour-based absorption loads a heavy overhead on small pieces; ABC would trace overhead to the activities each item actually consumes and show whether the pillow items really cost that much.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Which line feeds which in the order sheet, and which way the per-piece cost and profit move when an input changes.

questions.q: Fabric in A-grade pieces (metres) is calculated as:
questions.explain: 1,776 pieces × 0.43 m = 763.68 m. Dividing by the rating would give pieces per metre, and multiplying by the fabric rate gives rupees, not metres.

questions.q: Total variable manufacturing cost of an item equals:
options: Fabric cost + accessories + labour + loading − B-grade proceeds − rag proceeds
Fabric cost + accessories + labour + loading + B-grade proceeds + rag proceeds
questions.explain: The two proceeds are credits, so they reduce the cost; everything else is added. Option 2 is the common error of treating proceeds as costs.

questions.q: If the linear rating of an item rises from 0.43 m to 0.45 m with everything else unchanged, the fabric cost per piece will:
options: Fall, because fewer pieces are cut
Rise in proportion to the rating
Stay the same, because the fabric rate is unchanged
questions.explain: Fabric per piece is rating × rate; a higher rating means more metres per piece and so a higher fabric cost per piece. The rate per metre has not changed, but the metres have.

questions.q: Doubling the direct labour per piece (with the 3.2 multiplier unchanged) will:
options: Double the labour cost but leave fixed cost allocated unchanged
Double both the labour cost and the fixed cost allocated
Double the fixed cost allocated only
Change nothing, because labour is a fixed cost
questions.explain: Fixed cost allocated = 3.2 × direct labour, so it moves with labour; a labour-heavy piece therefore carries a doubly heavy burden — the point the lecture makes about pillow items.

questions.q: Rag proceeds in rupees are calculated as:
questions.explain: Rags are sold by the metre at 15 % of the fabric rate: 25 m × 0.15 × Rs 167 = Rs 626.25. 15 % of the whole fabric cost would be Rs 19,864 — far too much.

questions.q: If the sales price of an item is below its total variable cost per piece, the item loses money even before any fixed cost is allocated.
questions.explain: Contribution = price − variable cost; if that is negative the item cannot cover any overhead at all. The pillow case 20×32 at Rs 80 against a variable cost of Rs 85.42 is exactly this case.

questions.q: The total profit or loss of an item in the sheet is found by:
questions.explain: (Rs 80 − Rs 89.26) × 1,776 = −Rs 16,449. B-grade pieces are not sold at the order price, so they are excluded; their proceeds were already credited to fabric cost.

questions.q: Wastage in the sheet is defined as:
options: 1 − yield, i.e. the share of fabric not in A-grade pieces
questions.explain: Wastage = 1 − yield = 3.7 % for the pillow case, covering both the B-grade fabric and the rags. Rags alone would be 25 ÷ 792.98 = 3.2 %.

questions.q: Raising the B-grade proceed per piece from Rs 15 to Rs 30 will:
options: Lower the total variable cost of the item
Raise the total variable cost of the item
Have no effect on the A-grade cost per piece
questions.explain: Proceeds are deducted from cost; a higher recovery on the 10 B-grade pieces lowers the net cost spread over the A-grade pieces, though by only Rs 150 ÷ 1,776 ≈ Rs 0.08 each.

questions.q: The per-piece total cost in the sheet is:
options: Total cost of the order ÷ A-grade pieces
Total cost of the order ÷ fabric consumed
Variable cost per piece − fixed cost per piece
Sales price − profit per piece, which cannot be computed from the sheet
questions.explain: Rs 158,529.45 ÷ 1,776 = Rs 89.26, the figure that is compared with the Rs 80 price. Option 4 is numerically true but it is the profit that is derived from the cost, not the reverse.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Costing a pillow sham and a comforter shell line by line, from fabric consumed to cost per piece and the order's profit or loss.

questions.q: A pillow sham has a linear rating of 0.48 m per piece. How many metres of fabric are in 2,000 A-grade pieces?
questions.explain: Fabric in A-grade pieces = 2,000 × 0.48 = 960 m.

questions.q: The same sham order also produced 12 B-grade pieces (rating 0.48 m) and 30 m of rags. Fabric in A-grade pieces is 960 m. What is the total fabric consumed, to two decimal places?
Fabric in A-grade pieces is 960 m out of 995.76 m consumed. What is the yield as a percentage, to one decimal place?
questions.explain: Yield = 960 ÷ 995.76 = 0.9641 = 96.4 %; wastage is therefore 3.6 %.

questions.q: 995.76 m of fabric is consumed at a rate of Rs 180 per linear metre. What is the fabric cost, to the nearest rupee?
30 m of rags are sold at 15 % of the fabric rate of Rs 180 per metre. What are the rag proceeds?
questions.explain: Rag proceeds = 30 × 0.15 × 180 = Rs 810, credited against the fabric cost.

questions.q: In the lecture's pillow-case line the fabric cost is Rs 132,427.66 for 1,776 A-grade pieces. What is the fabric cost per A-grade piece, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: 132,427.66 ÷ 1,776 = Rs 74.57 per A-grade piece, as in the sheet.

questions.q: Direct labour on a sham is Rs 1.50 per piece and fixed cost is allocated at 3.2 × direct labour. What is the fixed cost allocated per piece?
questions.explain: Fixed cost per piece = 3.2 × 1.50 = Rs 4.80.

questions.q: A comforter shell has a rating of 5.49 m at Rs 150 per metre, accessories Rs 40 per piece, direct labour Rs 12 per piece and fixed cost at 3.2 × labour. Ignoring proceeds and loading, what is the total cost per piece, to the nearest paisa?
questions.explain: Fabric 5.49 × 150 = 823.50; + accessories 40 + labour 12 + fixed 38.40 = Rs 913.90 per piece.

questions.q: The comforter shell above costs Rs 913.90 per piece and sells at Rs 900. The profit per piece is:
questions.explain: 900 − 913.90 = −13.90, a loss. Option 4 ignores accessories, labour and fixed cost; option 3 is just the fixed-cost line.

questions.q: The lecture's pillow case has a total order cost of Rs 158,529.45 and 1,776 A-grade pieces sold at Rs 80. The total loss on the item is nearest to:
questions.explain: Sales = 1,776 × 80 = Rs 142,080; loss = 158,529.45 − 142,080 = Rs 16,449.45. Rs 9.26 is the loss per piece, Rs 6,820 the allocated fixed cost.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions a stitching unit's costing office faces: pricing pillow items, handling B-grade and rags, and reading an order sheet that is profitable overall.

questions.q: A buyer asks for pillow cases only, at Rs 80, with the same costs as the lecture (total cost Rs 89.26 per piece). The costing office should:
options: Accept — the comforter lines will cover it
Decline or renegotiate — without the comforters there is nothing to cover the loss
Accept because fixed cost is not a real cost
Accept and raise the linear rating
questions.explain: The lecture's warning is that pillow cases must be priced on their own cost; the item does not even cover its variable cost of Rs 85.42, let alone overhead.

questions.q: Which action would most directly cut the fabric cost per piece of the pillow case?
options: Reducing the linear rating through a better marker or a smaller hem allowance
questions.explain: Fabric per piece is rating × rate; the rating is the only fabric input the stitching unit controls directly. Price changes profit but not cost.

questions.q: Rags from the pillow-case order rise from 25 m to 60 m because of a cutting fault. The effect on the sheet is:
options: Higher fabric consumed and cost, only partly offset by rag proceeds at 15 % of the rate
No effect, since rags are sold
Lower cost, because rags earn money
questions.explain: Every rag metre costs the full Rs 167 but recovers only Rs 25.05; the net loss is Rs 141.95 per metre, and yield falls.

questions.q: The order sheet shows the same comforter shell in Black losing Rs 22.64 per piece and in Stone earning Rs 29.53 at the same price. The most likely cause is:
options: A higher fabric rate per metre for the black dyed fabric
More pieces in the Stone order
questions.explain: Both lines have the same rating of 5.49 m and the same price of Rs 900 and 210 pieces; the cost difference of Rs 52 per piece comes from the fabric rate, dark shades costing more to dye.

questions.q: Because B-grade pieces are deducted as proceeds, producing more B-grade pieces improves the profit of an item.
questions.explain: A B-grade piece consumes a full rating of fabric, accessories and labour but recovers only Rs 15 against a price of Rs 80; every piece downgraded is a loss, not a gain.

questions.q: The merchandiser proposes quoting the whole eight-item order at one average price per piece. The costing office should object because:
options: Averages hide that pillow items lose money while comforters carry them; each item must be priced on its own cost
Averages are not allowed by the customer
The fabric rate is the same for all items
The fixed cost would then be zero
questions.explain: Per-piece costs range from Rs 89 to Rs 923; a single average price would under-price comforters and over-price pillows, and the mix could change on the next order.

questions.q: A manager argues that pillow items should not carry 3.2 × labour as overhead since they use little cutting-table and finishing time. The tool to settle this is:
options: Activity Based Costing, tracing overhead to the activities each item uses
questions.explain: This is the lecture's closing point: a labour-based absorption rate may overload small labour-heavy pieces; ABC checks whether the share is fair.

questions.q: Loading cost in the order sheet is entered as a total for the item. On a per-piece basis it is:
options: Divided over the A-grade pieces like the other totals
questions.explain: All order totals, loading included, are divided by A-grade pieces to reach the per-piece variable cost of Rs 85.42; only direct labour is multiplied by 3.2.

questions.q: A supervisor suggests saving labour on the pillow case by simplifying the hem, cutting direct labour from Rs 1.20 to Rs 1.00 per piece. Under the sheet's method the cost per piece falls by:
questions.explain: Labour falls by Rs 0.20 and allocated fixed cost by 3.2 × 0.20 = Rs 0.64, a total of Rs 0.84 — which shows how strongly the labour-based rate rewards labour savings on paper.

questions.q: The grand total of the order is a profit of Rs 240,693 on 8,852 pieces. A sensible reading of this is:
options: The order is fine; nothing needs attention
The order is acceptable overall, but the loss-making pillow items should be repriced before the next order
questions.explain: The lecture says the order is profitable only because of two comforter lines; the pillow items each lose money and should be priced on their own cost in future.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions on the order sheet: contribution before overhead, the price that breaks even, and the errors that make a losing item look fine.

questions.q: The pillow case sells at Rs 80 and its total variable cost per piece is Rs 85.42. What is the contribution per piece? Give a negative number for a negative contribution.
questions.explain: Contribution = 80 − 85.42 = −Rs 5.42: the pillow case does not cover its own variable cost, so no amount of fixed-cost reallocation can make it profitable at this price.

questions.q: The pillow case's total cost is Rs 89.26 per piece. What price would give a 10 % margin on cost, to the nearest paisa?
questions.explain: 89.26 × 1.10 = Rs 98.19 — about Rs 18 above the Rs 80 actually quoted.

questions.q: An order of 1,500 A-grade pieces has a rating of 0.54 m, 8 B-grade pieces and 20 m of rags, fabric at Rs 170 per metre. B-grade proceeds are Rs 15 per piece and rags fetch 15 % of the fabric rate. What is the net fabric cost after proceeds, to the nearest rupee?
A trainee computes the pillow case's fixed cost as 3.2 × the fabric cost. The result would be:
options: Correct, since fabric is the largest cost
Far too high — the multiplier applies to direct labour (Rs 2,131.20), giving Rs 6,819.84, not Rs 423,768
Too low, since fabric cost excludes proceeds
questions.explain: 3.2 × Rs 132,427.66 = Rs 423,768, about three times the whole sales value of the item; the sheet applies the multiplier to direct labour only.

questions.q: If the fixed-cost multiplier is cut from 3.2 to 2.0, the pillow case's total cost per piece becomes:
questions.explain: Fixed cost per piece = 2.0 × 1.20 = Rs 2.40 instead of Rs 3.84; total = 85.42 + 2.40 = Rs 87.82, still above the Rs 80 price.

questions.q: If the multiplier were set to zero, the pillow case at Rs 80 would show a profit.
questions.explain: With no fixed cost at all the cost is the variable Rs 85.42 per piece, still Rs 5.42 above the price; the loss is not caused by the overhead allocation alone.

questions.q: In the eight-item order the Stone comforter shell 91×91 earns Rs 169.86 per piece on 1,000 pieces, and the Black pillow sham 20×36 loses Rs 3.37 per piece on 2,016 pieces. What is the combined profit of these two lines, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: 169,860 − 6,793.92 = Rs 163,066.08 — one comforter line more than absorbs the sham's loss, which is why the order total looks healthy.

questions.q: Which statement about the pillow case line is correct?
options: Its wastage of 3.7 % is made up entirely of rags
Its B-grade fabric (4.30 m) is 10 pieces × 0.43 m
Its loading cost is multiplied by 3.2
Its rag proceeds equal 15 % of the fabric cost
questions.explain: 4.30 ÷ 0.43 = 10 B-grade pieces. Wastage includes those 4.30 m as well as the 25 m of rags; rag proceeds are 15 % of the rate on rag metres only.

questions.q: The pillow case line would just break even at Rs 80 if the total cost per piece fell by Rs 9.26. Which single change comes closest to achieving that?
options: Cutting the linear rating from 0.43 m to 0.38 m (saving about Rs 8.35 of fabric)
questions.explain: Accessories at Rs 10 per piece exceed the Rs 9.26 gap; the rating cut saves 0.05 × 167 = Rs 8.35, not quite enough; proceeds and loading are worth well under Rs 1 per piece. Of course accessories cannot really be removed — the point is to see where the cost lies.

questions.q: A costing clerk divides the total cost by A-grade plus B-grade pieces (1,786) instead of A-grade pieces only. The per-piece cost will appear:
options: Slightly lower than the true Rs 89.26, flattering the item
questions.explain: 158,529.45 ÷ 1,786 = Rs 88.76 — lower, because the cost is spread over pieces that will not be sold at Rs 80. Only A-grade pieces earn the price, so only they should carry the cost.
